Brent Crashes 7% on Iran Peace Hopes Despite Fresh Saudi Pipeline Attack

Another round of unconfirmed reports about a potential U.S.-Iran diplomatic breakthrough sent fresh optimism rippling through oil markets on Monday, after Al Arabiya claimed that a Qatari-Pakistani mediation proposal had revived serious negotiations over Tehran's nuclear program.

Citing unnamed sources, Al Arabiya reported that Washington was prepared to allow Iran to continue enriching uranium to 3.67%, with Tehran supposedly agreeing to the proposed limit. The sources suggested that a preliminary agreement was increasingly likely, although neither side has publicly acknowledged such a breakthrough.

There were also claims that arrangements were underway to discuss the return of International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors to Iran, despite no clarity over the scope of their inspections or the conditions under which they would operate.

Crucially, neither Washington nor Tehran has confirmed the reported enrichment agreement, while a senior Qatari official has reportedly disputed details of the proposal. The suggested 3.67% enrichment threshold would represent a significant reduction from the 60% levels Iran has previously achieved, effectively returning to the limit established under the 2015 nuclear agreement. Such a major concession would be difficult to reconcile with the increasingly uncompromising rhetoric coming from both sides, raising questions about whether the latest reports represent genuine diplomatic progress or another round of premature speculation.

The reports follow renewed diplomatic efforts involving Qatar and Pakistan, with Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani scheduled to meet President Donald Trump on Monday to discuss a possible ceasefire and renewed nuclear negotiations.

However, the latest optimism contrasts sharply with comments from U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio over the weekend.

Speaking to reporters Sunday, Rubio dismissed suggestions of an imminent breakthrough, saying Tehran's demands were "not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous."

Rubio acknowledged that Washington remained open to diplomacy but warned that negotiations had so far produced little meaningful progress.

Oil markets have already demonstrated how sensitive they are to unconfirmed diplomatic headlines.

Last Wednesday, Brent crude plunged nearly 9%, falling below $95 per barrel amid expectations that the Democratic sweep of Congress would accelerate an end to the Iran war.

The selloff was amplified by reports from Al Jadeed claiming significant progress in U.S.-Iran negotiations, claims that were subsequently rejected by a senior Iranian official.

Meanwhile, attacks on critical Middle Eastern energy infrastructure continue despite the diplomatic maneuvering.

Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy confirmed Monday that its strategically important East-West oil pipeline was targeted in the Medina region, triggering a limited fire.

Emergency crews extinguished the blaze, and authorities reported no casualties or disruption to pipeline operations.

The pipeline is particularly important because it allows Saudi Arabia to export crude through the Red Sea, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.

The contrasting developments underscore the uncertainty facing oil markets: while diplomatic progress could eventually restore Middle Eastern energy flows, continued attacks on vital infrastructure suggest that the geopolitical risk premium is unlikely to disappear overnight.
